newsitem.title: USA: AT&T simplifies card plan, adds payphone fee.
newsitem.headline: AT&T simplifies card plan, adds payphone fee.

text.p: AT&T Corp introduced a flat, $0.35 per-minute charge for phone calls using its AT&T calling card and cut the surcharges customers pay for connecting to the AT&T network, a spokeswoman said.
Separately, the leading U.S. long distance carrier said it will add a $0.35 charge for coinless calls made from payphones over the AT&T network in order to meet new U.S. regulations.

The charge is designed to offset compensation payments it and other long distance carriers are now required to make to payphone operators according to a U.S. Federal Communications Commission order handed down last fall.
AT&T said the company will see no benefit from its new $0.35 payhone fee and additional charges it levelled on business customers earlier this year.
AT&T has had business customers, not consumers, bear the lion's share of the burden for the payphone compensation, according to industry sources.
In February, AT&T boosted 1-800 number rates by three percent on businesses for incoming customer calls and added a $0.15 per call surcharge on business calling cards.
On May 1, it raised rates for interstate toll-free service seven percent and for outgoing business calls by two percent.
All revenue collected by AT&T from these fees will be used to offset rebates it is paying to payphone operators. "Not a nickel will land in our pockets," a spokeswoman stressed.

AT&T spokeswoman Karyn Vaughn-Fritz said the switch to per-minute charges has replaced a complicated hodgepodge of up to 66 factors previously used to set pricing, including the time of day of the call and the distance it travelled.
The AT&T network access charge cuts also cover holders of calling cards from local exchange carriers that have reciprocal agreements with AT&T, the spokeswoman said.
The switch to per-minute pricing, combined with the lower network surcharge costs, will mean a one percent overall cut in an average AT&T customer's costs, Vaughn-Fritz said.

In a move analysts said was designed to shore up AT&T customer loyalty, calling card customers dialing a special "800" number (1 800 CALLATT) will pay a one-time network access charge of $0.35, down from the prior $0.90 surcharge.

AT&T card customers direct dialing using the 0+ prefix will pay a $0.60 surcharge, down from $0.90. Holders of other cards accepted by AT&T will pay a $0.95 access surcharge, down from the previous fee of $1.20.

AT&T consumer card pricing changes became effective May 27 but were not publicly announced. The company plans to trumpet the changes through a direct-mail campaign and full-page newspaper ads that will begin rolling out next week.

The FCC order calls on 20 long distance operators to refund about $1 billion to payphone operators. AT&T must shoulder a little over 50 percent of that amount, reflecting AT&T's estimated share of the payphone long distance market.

The 1996 Telecom Act included clauses to allow payphone operators, which are mostly regional Bells, but also include a number of independent telephone companies, to be compensated for non-coin calls made from their payphones.

The FCC plan requires long distance carriers to compensate qualifying public payphone owners for coinless calls including consumer calling card, collect, credit card and operator- andled calls. AT&T's current share of the cost is $26.21 per public payphone per month.

AT&T has appealed the FCC order, arguing the amount it must compensate payphone operators is too high. AT&T has pledged to roll back the new payphone fee if it succeeeds in cutting back what it rebates to payphone companies, an official said.
In February, AT&T adjusted its business customer rates by adding a $0.15 per payphone call charge to recover costs for payphone compensation.
AT&T shares were off $1 at 35-3/8 at mid-afternoon Friday.
